Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 100, verse 1:

Surat al-ʿĀdiyāt

Makki according to the view of Ibn Masʿud, Jabir, al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah and ʿAta'; Madani according to the view of Anas, Qatadah and one of the two reports from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out cavalry, and they remained away for a month without any news reaching him from them, so the following was revealed: ﴿By the racers﴾, and so on."

Its number of verses is eleven, without disagreement.

Abu ʿUbayd, in his Fada'il, transmitted from the mursal report of al-Hasan that it is equal to half the Qur'an. Muhammad ibn Nasr transmitted the same from the route of ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), but I have not come upon its secret. When [Allah, glorified is He,] mentioned in the preceding surah the recompense for good and evil, He followed it in this one with the torment of those who preferred their worldly life over their hereafter and did not prepare for it by doing good. The connection, or relationship, between His words there, ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾, and His words here, ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾, is not hidden, according to what you have heard, that the intended "burdens" are the dead within it, or what encompasses them and the treasures.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿By the racers﴾: the majority hold that it is an oath by the horses of the warriors in the path of Allah, which run (taʿduw), that is, which move swiftly toward the enemy. The origin of al-ʿAdiyat is al-ʿAduwat with a waw, which was changed to a yaʾ because of the kasra before it.

His words, [Exalted is He]: ﴿ḍabhan﴾ is a verbal noun in the accusative, governed by its omitted verb, meaning: they snort (tadhbahu) or they snort a snorting (yadhbahna ḍabhan). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). Its ḍabh is the sound of their breaths as they run. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: when horses run, they say "ihh ihh," and that is their ḍabh.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face: the ḍabh of horses is the hamhamah, and of camels is the breathing (tanaffus).

In al-Bahr: it is a loud vocalization during intense running, which is neither a neigh, nor a bray, nor a bark, but rather a sound other than the usual sound of the animal to which it is attributed. From Ibn ʿAbbas: among animals, only horses and dogs snort; but this is not authentically established from him, for the Arabs used ḍabh for camels, for black snakes, for owls, for hares and for foxes, and sometimes they ascribe it to the bow. Abu Hanifah recited in its description:

A bowstring of the nasham or talib, snorting in the hand like the barking of a fox.

Some have mentioned that its origin is for the fox, and it was borrowed for horses, as in the words of ʿAntarah:

And the horses strive when they snort (tadbahu) at the watering-places of death, a snorting.

And it is said that it is from "dabahtahu al-nar," meaning the fire changed its color without greatly affecting it. It is said: "indhabaha lawnuhu," meaning his color changed slightly toward blackness. Abu ʿUbaydah said:

Ḍabh, and likewise ḍabʿ, mean intense running. On this basis it has been said that it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of al-ʿAdiyat, and there is no implied verb. It is also permitted, on the interpretation given above, that it be in the accusative as a verbal noun as well, but on the basis that running necessarily entails snorting, so it has the force of the verb "to snort." It may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative, interpreted as an active participle, on the basis that the original in such cases is that they are not fixed nouns; that is, "and the racers, snorting."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 100, verse 2:

﴿Then those that strike sparks with their hooves﴾. Al-Iwra' (striking forth fire) is bringing out fire, and al-qadh (striking) is hitting and knocking, as is well known. It is said: "qadaha fa-awra" (he struck and so brought out fire) when he struck and brought out the fire, and "qadaha fa-asladh" (he struck but did not bring it out) when he struck but did not bring it out. The meaning here is also the horses; that is, those which strike fire from the impact of their hooves against the stones. That fire is called "nar al-habahib" (the fire of al-Habahib), and al-Habahib is the name of a stingy man who would kindle only a weak fire out of fear of guests, so they made him a proverb, until they said this of what horses strike with their hooves and camels with their soft pads.

The accusative of "qadhan" is like the accusative of "dhabhan" as previously mentioned. It has also been permitted that it be a specifier (tamyiz) transferred from the subject; that is, "fa-al-mawri qadhuha" (so the one that strikes forth fire is its striking), and perhaps this is more eloquent and further from the sense of "striking."

And from Qatadah: "al-muriyat" is a metaphor for horses that kindle and ignite the fire of war, and this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 100, verse 3:

﴿Then by those that charge[1]﴾ — from aghara 'ala al-'aduww, meaning to fall upon the enemy suddenly with one's horses, for plunder, killing, or taking captives. So the ghara (raid) is an attribute of the owners of horses, and its attribution to the horses is either by way of metonymy (tajawwuz) in it, or by the omission of a modifier (taqdir al-mudaf). The original is "fa-al-mughir ashabuha," i.e., "those (horses) whose riders charge upon the enemy with them." It has also been said: "by means of them." ﴿at dawn﴾, i.e., at the time of subh (dawn), so it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyyah). That is the custom in raids: they would travel by night so that the enemy would not perceive them, and they would attack in the morning so that they could see what they were doing and what they were leaving. They would take pride in this, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"My people, those who attacked the morning
on the day of al-Nakhil, a raid, persistent"

[1] "Charge" translates al-mughirat; "ghara" (raid) denotes a sudden assault, and "tajawwuz" (metonymy) and "taqdir al-mudaf" (an elided modifier) are grammatical devices explained by the commentator.

Page 216

﴿Then raise thereby﴾ from al-ithara (stirring up), which is inciting and stirring up dust or the like. The original form was ath-wara-na: the vowel of the waw was moved to the letter before it, the waw was changed into an alif and deleted because two unvowelled letters came together. The verb is coordinated with the noun before it, which is "al-'adiyat" (the chargers), or with what follows it, because it is an active participle and has the meaning of a verb, especially when it occurs as a relative clause. So it is as if it were said: "those who ran, then struck sparks, then attacked at dawn, then raised..." There is no irregularity in such a construction, since the verb is a follower (in the sense of a coordinated element), so it does not require the article "al" to enter upon it; and there is no need to say that it is coordinated with a verb that stood in place of the active participle. The wisdom in this verb coming after an active participle, according to what Ibn al-Munayyir said, is to depict these actions in the mind; depiction is achieved by placing the verb after the noun, because of the contrast between them, and this is more eloquent than depiction by consistent nouns. Likewise, depiction by the present tense after the present tense, as in the words of Ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"That I have met the ghoul, descending with grey-white (horses) like a page, a wide plain..."

"So I seize him, and I strike him, and he falls, a prostrate one, on his hands and on his neck."

The benefit of this position, according to al-Tibi, is that the horses were described with the three attributes so that there would be arranged upon them what was intended of victory through conquest. So the past verb and what follows it are brought as consequences of the agent-nouns, and this shows that this persistence produced these two aims. It is understood from this that the fa' (then) is for ordering what follows from what precedes and making it a consequence of it; the discussion of it will come shortly, God willing.

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the dawn, and the ba' is for time, meaning: they stirred up at that time "naq'an", that is, dust. The restriction of its stirring to the dawn is because it does not stir, or its stirring is not evident, at night; and by this it becomes clear that the attack which is not seen in daytime occurs at night. In the mention of the stirring of dust there is an indication, without dust, of the intensity of the running and the abundance of advance and retreat, and they often point to this by it. From it is the saying of Ibn Rawaha:

"May I lose my little daughter if you do not see them stirring dust from the two sides of Kada..."

Abu 'Ubayda said: al-naq' is the raising of the voice. From it is the saying of Labid:

"So when a true cry rises, they milk it, having a sound and a clamour..."

And the saying of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, when it was said to him on the day Khalid ibn al-Walid died that the women had gathered weeping over Khalid: "What is it to the women of Banu al-Mughira that they should pour out their tears for Abu Sulayman while they sit, so long as there is no naq' (raised cry) nor laqlaqa (wailing)."

According to this meaning, the sense is: they raised, at that time, a shout, which is the shout of one who is attacked and struck. The well-known meaning is the first, and it is permitted that the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the enemy indicated by "al-'adiyat", or to the raid indicated by "al-mughirat", and the masculine form is due to interpreting it as running and the like; the ba' is causal or for accompaniment. It is also permitted that it be for time, with the pronoun referring to the place indicated by the context. The first is more evident and more subtle.

Similarly, the pronoun "bihi" (in it/with it) in His words, Mighty and Majestic be He: ﴿fa-wasaṭna bihi﴾ (and so they cut through it), meaning: they penetrated, at that very time, ﴿jam'an﴾ (a mass) of the enemy's throngs. It is also permitted to read the pronoun and the preposition bā' (the "bi") in it in the same manner as what preceded in "bihi" before it.

It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to al-naq' (the dust cloud) and the bā' is for accompaniment (mulabasah), meaning: they penetrated, accompanied by the dust cloud, as a mass. Or, according to what has been said, the bā' is for transitivity (ta'diyah), if it is meant that they caused the dust to cut through (the throng). The fa's (the successive particles) are as in al-Irshad, to indicate the sequence of what follows each of them upon what precedes it: so the penetration of the mass is consequent upon the stirring up (of dust), which is consequent upon the charging, which is consequent upon the running.

Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "fa-aththarna" and "fa-wassaṭna" with the thā' and the sīn doubled (shaddah). 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), Zayd ibn 'Ali, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Layla read the first (fa-aththarna) as the majority reads it, and the second (fa-wassaṭna) as those two read it. The meaning with the doubling of the first is: "they made dust appear by it," because the effect (ta'thir) in it carries the sense of making appear (al-izhar). With the doubling of the second, it is according to what preceded. They have transmitted that wasaṭa, both lightened and doubled, carry one meaning, and that they are two dialects. Ibn Jinni said: the meaning is "they separated by it a mass," i.e., they made it two halves, two parts.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the doubling in it is for transitivity, and the bā' is superfluous for emphasis, as in His words, Exalted is He: "and they brought it" in one reading; and it is an intensification of "wasaṭna." It is also permitted that the form be altered from "thawarna" to "watharna," then the waw was changed into a hamzah, so the meaning is as has passed; but this is a strained interpretation which is unnecessary.

From al-Suddi, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that they said: al-'adiyat (the charging ones) are camels that run with snorting (dabh) from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and from Muzdalifah to Mina. This is attributed to 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face). Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in Kitab al-Addad, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "While I was sitting in al-Hijr, a man came to me and asked me about (al-'adiyati dabha) 'the charging ones snorting.' I said: 'They are horses when they raid in the way of Allah, then they return at night, and they prepare their food and kindle their fire.' He turned away from me and went to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was sitting under the water-fountain of Zamzam. He asked him about al-'adiyati dabha, and he said: 'Have you asked anyone about it before me?' He said: 'Yes. I asked Ibn 'Abbas about it.'

He said: 'They are horses when they raid in the way of Allah.' 'Ali said: 'Go and call him for me.' When I stood over his head, he said: 'You give fatwas to people about what you have no knowledge of! By Allah, if they were indeed the first raid in Islam, it was Badr, and there were only two horses with us: a horse of al-Zubayr and a horse of al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. So how could the charging ones be snorting? Rather, al-'adiyati dabha are camels that run from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and when they return to Muzdalifah, they kindle fires.'"

﴿fa-l-mughirati subhan﴾ (then the raiders at dawn) from Muzdalifah to Mina; that is the "jam'" (mass). As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-atharna bihi naq'an﴾ (and raised up dust by it), it is the dust of the ground when they trample it with their hooves. Ibn 'Abbas said: "So I withdrew from my statement to the statement of 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and may Allah be pleased with him."

It was objected to his (i.e., 'Ali's) response, may Allah ennoble his face, that the intended meaning is horses, given the matter of the Battle of Badr, on the grounds that Ibn 'Abbas did not claim that the alif-lam in al-'adiyat is for specific reference, and that it refers to the charging horses of Badr, nor that the surah was revealed concerning that raid, so that it would necessarily follow that this is realized in it and that it falls under the generality; rather, the apparent sense of his words is to take it as the genus of horses that run in the way of Allah, Mighty and Majestic be He, even if it were taken as specific reference. It has been said: the known thing is the horses which the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him sent out for the raid, as you heard at the beginning of the surah; and likewise on what is related: "that he, Prayer and Peace be upon him, sent a detachment to some people of Banu Kinanah and appointed over them al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, who was one of the nuqaba', and its news was delayed from the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him for a month, so the hypocrites said: 'They have been killed,' and so the surah was revealed informing him, Prayer and Peace be upon him, of their safety and giving him good news of their raid upon the people," is not far-fetched. It is answered that he, may Allah ennoble his face, meant that the Battle of Badr is the most excellent of the raids of Islam, and its Badr is the one in which there is no breach, so it is necessary that it not be the intended meaning. The verse is to be taken in whatever manner suits it among the paths. It is not hidden that this answer does not bear, due to its great weakness, the attack upon it nor the loosing of the reins of the charging thoughts toward it; and the more fitting view is that the report has no soundness, and al-Hakim's authentication is judged against by the people of transmission, due to his great leniency in it, and that it is not reliable. Then, the report from him, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the meaning of al-'adiyat contradicts what preceded, that they are the camels of the pilgrims. The author of al-Ta'wilat reported that he, may Allah ennoble his face, explained them as the camels of Badr, and that Ibn Mas'ud was the one who explained them as the camels of the pilgrims. What favors the meaning of horses is that the raising of dust is more apparent in them than in camels. Moreover, that report requires that the thing sworn by be two kinds: horses and camels, and the company of raiders or pilgrims kindling fire for their food or the like. In some reports from Ibn 'Abbas there is something clearer than what preceded in the explanation of al-muriyat, in a manner that differs from al-'adiyat in essence: in al-Bahr from him that they are the company that kindles its fire at night for its need and its food. In another narration from him: they are the company of raiders who kindle much fire to terrify. The difference has also been related from others. From Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam, and this is another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, they are the company that plots in war; the Arabs say when they wish to deceive a man: "By Allah, I will kindle [deceit] for him." Among the strange things related from 'Ikrimah is that they are the tongues of men that kindle fire from the great things that are spoken, and what becomes apparent from proofs and arguments, and the manifestation of truth and the nullification of falsehood. But it is as you see.

Among the inner meanings and allusions: that the thing sworn by is the charging souls, following their perfection, the ones that kindle with their thoughts the lights of knowledge, and that charge upon desire and habits, when there appears to them the like of the lights of holiness, so they raise by it longing, and cut through by that longing a mass of the hosts of the "Illiyyin." Similar to this is what has been said: that this is an oath by the lofty resolves of the body, which run in the way of Allah, Exalted is He, bringing forth from the depth of their yearning the sound of supplication, from the intensity of the running and the utmost of longing, such that the spiritual beings hear the clamor of their supplication, their humbling, and their request for the facilitation of traversing the rugged path, which is attached to the mountains of the body. The ones that kindle with the hoofs of remembrance the fire of guidance hidden in the recess of the body at the time of the leavening of the subtle faculty; and the ones that charge, after their passage through the mountains of the body, firm in the darkness of the bodily night, and their crossing from it toward the horizon of the world of the soul, and the breathing of the dawn of the soul upon the psychic thoughts and their affairs. So by that running they stir up the dust of the thoughts and raise it, lest any thought be hidden; and so they cut through by that a mass of the hosts of the heart's faculties and the party of the remembrance-thoughts, which is the party of the Merciful in the midst of the world of the soul. And for them in this domain there is other than that.

Whatever the case, the thing sworn to

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 100, verse 6:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ — that is, ungrateful and ungrateful in denial, from kanada (kanada al-ni'mah), meaning he denied the blessing, covered it over, and did not give thanks for it. And they recited:

Ungrateful to the favours of men, and whoever is ungrateful to the favours of men will be distanced.

And from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil: al-kanud, in the language of Kindah and Hadramawt, means the disobedient; in the language of Rabi'ah and Mudar, the ungrateful; in the language of Kinanah, the miserly who has bad ownership (malakah). From this comes the phrase "barren land" (al-ardh al-kanud), which produces nothing. Al-Kalbi said something similar, except that he said: and in the language of Banu Malik, the miserly; and he did not mention Hadramawt, but confined himself to Kindah.

Interpreting it here as "ungrateful" is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Ibn 'Asakir recorded it from Abu Umamah, traced back (marfu') to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

In another narration from al-Hasan, he said: It is one who blames his Lord, mighty and majestic, counting the misdeeds and forgetting the good deeds.

Al-Tabarani and others narrated, with a weak chain, from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do you know what the kanud is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is the ungrateful one who beats his servant, withholds his gift, and eats alone."

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad and al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and others recorded its interpretation as one who withholds his gift, dwells alone, and beats his servant, as a statement (mawquf) of Abu Umamah. The majority hold to interpreting it as "ungrateful," and each of what has been mentioned does not escape ingratitude, and intensified ingratitude gathers various kinds of it. The alif-lam in "al-insan" is for the genus, and the judgment upon it with what has been mentioned is by consideration of some of the individuals.

It has been said: what is meant is a specific disbeliever, based on what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed about Qurt ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Nawfal al-Qurashi, and it is supported by His words after it: ﴿Does he not know?﴾ etc., since that befits only the disbeliever. But there is scrutiny in both matters. It has been said: what is meant is all people, in the sense that human nature drives him to that, except when Allah protects him from it by His gentleness and success. Izz al-Din (Isam al-Din) chose this and said: in it is praise for the warriors (ghuzat) for their striving against their natural disposition. And "li-rabbihi" is connected to "kanud," and the lam does not prevent that; it was placed first for the sake of the verse-ending (fasilah) while being more important, since the severe blame is upon ingratitude for His blessing, mighty and majestic. It has also been said that it is for restriction (takhsis) by way of emphasis.

[p. 219]

And "innahu" refers to *al-insan* (the human being), as al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said. ﴿Upon that﴾, i.e., upon his ingratitude (*kunud*), ﴿is a witness﴾, because the effect of it is evident upon him. So the testimony is by the tongue of the state (*lisan al-hal*), which is more eloquent than the tongue of speech (*lisan al-maqal*). It was also said: it is by the tongue of speech, but in the Hereafter. It was also said: *shahid* here derives from *shuhud* (witnessing/being present), not from *shahadah* (testimony), in the sense that he is ungrateful while knowing his ingratitude, and that doing evil while knowing it is the utmost blame. The first view is the apparent one.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: the pronoun in "innahu" refers to God, Exalted is He; that is, "Indeed, His Lord is a witness against him," so the statement is in the manner of a threat (*wa'id*). Al-Tibrizi preferred this and said: "It is the more correct, because the pronoun must return to the nearest preceding noun." It is objected that this obligation is not granted, and the consistency of pronouns and their not being broken up favours the first view. For the earlier pronoun, namely the pronoun in ﴿to his Lord﴾, refers to the human being necessarily, and likewise the following pronoun, namely the pronoun in God's words, ﴿And indeed he is, for the love of good﴾, i.e., of wealth,
[p. 219 continues]
and this meaning occurs in the Qur'an many times, to the extent that 'Ikrimah claimed that *khayr* wherever it occurs in the Qur'an means wealth. Some restricted it to abundant wealth, and it was explained thus in God's words, ﴿if he leaves behind good (*khayran*), the bequest﴾. The description of it as "good" is according to what people see; otherwise, some of it is evil on the Day of Resurrection. The lam here indicates causation, i.e., "indeed, he is, because of his love of wealth, ﴿intensely (*shadid*)﴾," i.e., stingy, as it is said. Just as the stingy person is called *shadid*, he is also called *mutashaddid*, as in the words of Tarafah:

"I see death selecting the noble and choosing
the precious wealth of the vile, the stingy."

*Shadid* here may be in the sense of a passive participle (*maf'ul*): as if the stingy person has been tightened against generosity. It may also be in the sense of an active participle (*fa'il*): as if he has tightened his purse so that he brings nothing out of it. Others allowed that *shadid* means "strong," and this is perhaps the more apparent; and the lam, on this reading, is in the sense of *fi* ("in"): that is, "indeed he is strong and excessive in his love of wealth." The intended meaning is the intensity of his love for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is: "And indeed he is, for love of wealth and preference for this world and seeking it, strong and capable; but for love of worshipping God and thanking His favour, Exalted is He, he is weak and sluggish. You say: 'He is *shadid* (strong) for this matter and *qawi* (powerful) for it' when he is capable of it and in control of it." Al-Nisaburi made the lam here one of causation, but this is not apparent. So consider.

Al-Farra' said: it is possible that the meaning is: "And indeed he is, for love of good, truly intense in love," meaning that he loves wealth and loves being one who loves it, but he has been content with the first love over the second, as God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿The wind has driven against it on a stormy day﴾, i.e., on a day of stormy wind, so he was content with the first over the second. Qutrub said: i.e., "indeed he is intense for love of good," as in your saying: "Indeed he is a striker for Zayd" versus "indeed he is a striker of Zayd." The apparent sense of the example is that he took the love of good as the direct object of *shadid*, that *shadid* is an active participle formed on the pattern *fa'il* for emphasis, and that the lam in ﴿for love﴾ is for reinforcement. There is much to be said about this.

It was also said: it is possible to consider *shadid* to be a sifah mushabbahah (an adjective of quality resembling an active participle), which was originally attached to its subject in the genitive, namely "love," which is attached to "good" in the manner of a verbal noun attached to its object. Then the attribution was reversed, the subject was put in the accusative by analogy with the direct object, then it was fronted and put in the genitive with the lam. Apart from the artificiality, there is the point that fronting the complement of an adjective before it is not permitted, and its being in the genitive in such a case does not help, since it is not in it in the way of "Zayd is glad with you," as is not hidden.

What is understood from al-Zamakhshari's words in *al-Kashshaf* is that it is permissible to take by "good" what is with God of acts of obedience, on the basis that the meaning is: "Indeed he is, for love of good things, not gentle and open, but rather tight and withdrawn."

For the earlier pronoun, namely the pronoun in ﴿to his Lord﴾, refers to the human being necessarily, and likewise the following pronoun, namely the pronoun in God's words, ﴿And indeed he is, for the love of good﴾, i.e., of wealth,
[p. 219 continues]
and this meaning occurs in the Qur'an many times, to the extent that 'Ikrimah claimed that *khayr* wherever it occurs in the Qur'an means wealth. Some restricted it to abundant wealth, and it was explained thus in God's words, ﴿if he leaves behind good (*khayran*), the bequest﴾. The description of it as "good" is according to what people see; otherwise, some of it is evil on the Day of Resurrection. The lam here indicates causation, i.e., "indeed, he is, because of his love of wealth, ﴿intensely (*shadid*)﴾," i.e., stingy, as it is said. Just as the stingy person is called *shadid*, he is also called *mutashaddid*, as in the words of Tarafah:

"I see death selecting the noble and choosing
the precious wealth of the vile, the stingy."

*Shadid* here may be in the sense of a passive participle (*maf'ul*): as if the stingy person has been tightened against generosity. It may also be in the sense of an active participle (*fa'il*): as if he has tightened his purse so that he brings nothing out of it. Others allowed that *shadid* means "strong," and this is perhaps the more apparent; and the lam, on this reading, is in the sense of *fi* ("in"): that is, "indeed he is strong and excessive in his love of wealth." The intended meaning is the intensity of his love for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is: "And indeed he is, for love of wealth and preference for this world and seeking it, strong and capable; but for love of worshipping God and thanking His favour, Exalted is He, he is weak and sluggish. You say: 'He is *shadid* (strong) for this matter and *qawi* (powerful) for it' when he is capable of it and in control of it." Al-Nisaburi made the lam here one of causation, but this is not apparent. So consider.

Al-Farra' said: it is possible that the meaning is: "And indeed he is, for love of good, truly intense in love," meaning that he loves wealth and loves being one who loves it, but he has been content with the first love over the second, as God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿The wind has driven against it on a stormy day﴾, i.e., on a day of stormy wind, so he was content with the first over the second. Qutrub said: i.e., "indeed he is intense for love of good," as in your saying: "Indeed he is a striker for Zayd" versus "indeed he is a striker of Zayd." The apparent sense of the example is that he took the love of good as the direct object of *shadid*, that *shadid* is an active participle formed on the pattern *fa'il* for emphasis, and that the lam in ﴿for love﴾ is for reinforcement. There is much to be said about this.

It was also said: it is possible to consider *shadid* to be a sifah mushabbahah (an adjective of quality resembling an active participle), which was originally attached to its subject in the genitive, namely "love," which is attached to "good" in the manner of a verbal noun attached to its object. Then the attribution was reversed, the subject was put in the accusative by analogy with the direct object, then it was fronted and put in the genitive with the lam. Apart from the artificiality, there is the point that fronting the complement of an adjective before it is not permitted, and its being in the genitive in such a case does not help, since it is not in it in the way of "Zayd is glad with you," as is not hidden.

What is understood from al-Zamakhshari's words in *al-Kashshaf* is that it is permissible to take by "good" what is with God of acts of obedience, on the basis that the meaning is: "Indeed he is, for love of good things, not gentle and open, but rather tight and withdrawn."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 100, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered forth﴾ and so on, is a warning and a threat. The hamza is for rebuke (inkar), and the fa' is for coordination with an implied antecedent which the context requires. The object of "yaʿlamu" (knows) is omitted, and it is the governing element of "idha" (when), which is a temporal adverb (zarfiyya). That is: Does he do what he does of foul deeds, or does he not take heed, so that he does not now know his end when those among the dead in the graves are scattered forth? And mentioning "ma" (what) rather than "man" (who) indicates that they, at that time, are far removed from the rank of rational beings.

Al-Hufi said: the governing element of "idha," the temporal one, is "yaʿlamu" (knows). It was objected to him that what is meant is not knowledge at that time but knowledge in this world. It was answered that this objection arises only if the pronoun in "yaʿlamu" refers to man, and that is not necessary according to this view, since it may refer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the two objects of "yaʿlamu" are then omitted.

The estimated sense is: Does Allah, exalted is He, not know them as doers of what they did when they are scattered forth? The knowledge is then a metaphor (kinaya) for recompense, and the meaning is: Will He not recompense them when they are scattered forth? The sentence that follows, which is emphatic, would then be a confirmation and establishment of this meaning. And that, as you see, is far-fetched.

It has been said: "idha" is the object of "yaʿlamu," in the sense: Does he not know that time and recognize its certainty? It has also been said that the element governing it is "buʿthira" (scattered forth), on the basis that it is conditional and not annexed (ghayr mudafa). They said: it was not permitted for "lakhabir" (surely aware) to govern it, because what follows "inna" does not govern what precedes it. The most correct of these views is what we have already mentioned. The transitivity of "ʿilm" (knowledge) when it means "maʿrifa" (recognition) to a single object is common, and the realization of the meaning of "buʿthara" (scattering) has already been discussed, so reflect upon it.

ʿAbd Allah read "buḥthira" with a ḥāʾ and a thāʾ with three dots.

al-Aswad ibn Zayd read "buḥith" with both of them, without a rāʾ. Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim read "buḥthira" like the reading of ʿAbd Allah, but in the active voice (lil-fa'il).

﴿And what is in the breasts is made manifest﴾ That is, what is in the hearts of firm resolves is gathered and brought out, just as the kernel is brought out of the husk. Either it is gathered, or its good is distinguished from its bad. So *hassala al-shay'* (to obtain, or to separate, a thing) has been used in the sense of distinguishing it from other things, as in *al-Bahr*. The root meaning of *tahsil* (extraction, separating out the essential part) is bringing the kernel out of the husk, like extracting gold from the ore and wheat from the chaff. The specification of what is in the hearts is because it is the origin of the actions of the limbs. For this reason, deeds are by intentions, and the first of thought is the last of action. So everything that is done follows it, and it indicates the whole, both explicitly and implicitly.

Ibn Ya'mur, Nasr ibn 'Asim and Muhammad ibn Abi Ma'dan read *"wa-hassala"* in the active voice, with its subject being His pronoun, may He be exalted and glorified.

Ibn Ya'mur and Nasr also read *"hasala"* in the active voice with a lightened *sad*, so that what is upon it (*ma 'alayhi*) is the subject.

**Qur'an 100:11:** ﴿Indeed, their Lord﴾ — i.e., those who are resurrected. After the second revival, He refers to them with the pronoun for rational beings (ḍamīr al-ʿuqalāʾ), having previously referred to them with *mā*, based on the difference between their two states.

﴿Concerning them﴾ — with respect to their essences, their attributes, and their conditions in all their details.

﴿On that Day﴾ — i.e., the day on which what was mentioned will occur: the raising of what is in the graves and the extraction of what is in the breasts. The two adverbial phrases (*al-ẓarfān*, temporal and locative complements) are connected to His saying, ﴿is All-Aware﴾ — i.e., He knows the outward and inward aspects of what they did, with a knowledge that necessitates recompense and is connected to it, as its restriction to that Day indicates. Otherwise, His knowledge, Mighty and Majestic is He, encompasses everything that has been and will be.

Abu al-Simmal and al-Ḥajjāj recited: *"Anna rabbahum bihim yawma'idhin khabīr"* (with the *hamza* of *anna* vowelled with a fatḥa and the emphatic *lām* omitted). In this reading, *anna* and what follows it constitute a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) in the position of an object of *yaʿlamu* (“He knows”), as some have inferred, and this is supported by the fact that *yaʿlamu* is suspended (*muʿallaqa*, i.e., its effect is blocked, governing a clause instead of a noun) from acting on *inna rabbahum* etc. in the reading of the majority, because of the presence of the *lām*. In that case, it is not permissible for the phrase to be connected to *khabīr* either, since it is in the description of the verbal *anna*, so its complement may not precede it. Its matter is known from what has preceded. It has been said that the statement is based on an implied *lām* of causation (*lām al-taʿlīl*), connected to *ḥuṣṣila* (“was extracted”), as if it were said: “and what is in the breasts was extracted, because their Lord is, concerning them, All-Aware on that Day.” The first view is more evident. And God Most High knows best and is most informed.
